title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (4 of 7)
hook: Death's answer: the self is not born and does not die
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, shreyas: the good and the pleasant both come to a person, and the wise choose the good.

If you read the Gita with us, today may bring a jolt of recognition. There's a verse you've heard before, in chapter two, when Krishna first tells Arjuna that the self can't be killed. Here it is again, almost word for word. Except now it isn't Krishna speaking on a battlefield. It's Death, speaking to a child. The Gita, it turns out, was borrowing from the Katha. Today Yama finally answers the question.
screen: `A VERSE YOU'VE HEARD BEFORE.` → `NOT KRISHNA. DEATH.` → `THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Yama says: the knowing self is not born, and does not die. It didn't come from anywhere, and it didn't become anyone. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient: it is not killed when the body is killed. Then: if the killer thinks he kills, and the killed thinks he's killed, neither of them understands. This one does not kill, and is not killed. Those two verses reappear in the Gita, two nineteen and two twenty, with small changes. So Death's answer to what happens when we die: the self you really are was never born, so it can't die. The body ends; the self doesn't. Then Yama adds something surprising about how this is known. The self is smaller than the small and greater than the great, hidden in the heart of every creature. It can't be gotten by lectures, or by brains, or by much learning. It's gained by the one it chooses; to that one it reveals its own nature. Commentators read that line differently. Shankara hears the seeker choosing the self alone. Theistic teachers like Ramanuja hear grace: the Lord chooses whom to reveal himself to. Both schools agree on the next line: not the one who hasn't turned from wrong, not the restless, not the scattered, can reach it by cleverness. That's why the two paths matter. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't a rule for its own sake. It's what makes the mind quiet enough to notice what was never born.
screen: `NOT BORN, AND DOES NOT DIE.` · `IT DOES NOT KILL; IT IS NOT KILLED.` · `NOT GAINED BY LEARNING.` · `THE ONE IT CHOOSES.` · then, large: `SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.`

segments.voice: Notice what in you has changed over the years: your body, your opinions, your face in photos. Then notice what hasn't, the plain sense of being here, aware, there at seven and here now, and rest in it for a few breaths. You don't have to decide what it is; it's simply the one thing in the room that didn't age.
Aja, unborn. The knowing self is not born, and does not die; it is not killed when the body is killed, unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Even Death answered the boy in the end. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Katha 1.2.18–19, echoed in Bhagavad Gita 2.19–20, is among the verses most often recited at Hindu funerals and memorials as the teaching that the self is not born and does not die.

fork.setup: Nachiketa asks what happens when a person dies. what does Death say?
options: 'the self is not born and does not die.'
fork.reveal: the knowing self was never born, so it isn't killed when the body is. the Gita repeats it.

original.note: Sanskrit: aja, unborn; Katha 1.2.18 calls the self unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita invented 'the self is never born'.
what it means: Death teaches it first, in the Katha, as the answer to the third wish.
what a scholar hears: Katha 1.2.18–19 closely match Gita 2.20 and 2.19; 1.2.23 ('the one it chooses') is read as grace by theistic Vedanta.
guess: reborn, coming back in a new life
recall: unknown to those who claim to know it
the ultimate reality, ground of all

chat.says: So what did Death finally tell the boy happens when we die?
options: That the self you really are was never born, so it isn't killed.
That nobody can know, so he sent the boy home without an answer.
That only those who learn enough scripture make it through death.
chat.meaning: Yama says the knowing self is not born and does not die; it is not killed when the body is killed.
